rows.evidence: Q1: sections 'ET-based irrigation scheduling and irrigation technology' and 'Corn to cotton conversion' (Eqs 1-8, Table VI, Figs 7-8): authors compute fraction of net irrigation requirement (FIR) from Agri-Partners field data and TWDB survey data and run their own scenario calculations of regional irrigation demand.
rows.notes: The study's own evidence does not support drip as a water-conserving measure. Table VI (Agri-Partners data, cotton only) shows SDI applied depth 274 mm and FIR 1.01, essentially identical to centre pivot (274 mm, FIR 1.03); the authors state explicitly that choosing SDI over spray or LEPA may not necessarily result in less irrigation demand, and SDI area was assumed negligible (fSDI = 0) in the demand-reduction scenarios. Statements that SDI gives greater yield, water use efficiency and warmer soil are citations of other work (Bordovsky and Porter 2003; Colaizzi et al. 2004-2006), not results of this study. Hence no own result showing drip delivers water conservation; the one own data point is a null result for one crop.

rows.evidence: Q1: sections 'ET-based irrigation scheduling and irrigation technology' (Eqs 1-6, Table VI, Fig 7): own computation of FIR from Agri-Partners demonstration data (about 20 000 ha, 450 fields) and TWDB county data, plus scenario runs. Q2: Table VI and following text: FIR of fields managed with the TXHPET network (Agri-Partners) was generally lower than FIR from TWDB data for the region, with yield seldom reduced, suggesting withdrawals could be reduced by greater adoption; Fig 7 and conclusions: doubling TXHPET-managed area from 40% to 80% (with gravity reduced to 10%) computed to cut demand by about 1 billion m3/yr (14%), up to 21% at full adoption. Q4: Eqs 2-5 and Table VI: the study computes the seasonal net irrigation requirement Ireq from ET network data (ETos x Kco minus precipitation) and the ratio of applied depth to requirement (FIR), i.e. the over-application relative to crop need through which ET scheduling reduces pumping. Q5: Table VI and Fig 7: FIR and demand reported separately for six crops (corn, cotton, sorghum, peanut, soybean, wheat) and for Northern and Southern High Plains districts. Q6: Agri-Partners FIR derived from commercial farms across the Northern High Plains (about 20 000 ha, 450 fields) and demand reductions computed for the 39-county region (Fig 7). Q8: text after Table VI: higher Agri-Partner yields may reflect greater management level of cooperators and USDA data may include damaged or grazed fields; TWDB volumes by irrigation technology were not available; applied depths may include conveyance losses; present TXHPET adoption (30-40%) is an estimate from subscriber numbers.
rows.notes: Technology match is approximate: the passage says weather-based scheduling, and the study concerns the TXHPET ET network disseminated by fax, email and internet, not a smartphone app. The Q2 evidence is observational and confounded (Agri-Partners cooperators are self-selected, better-managed fields compared with regional survey averages), and the regional savings figures are scenario calculations from assumed adoption rates. Q3 no: the Agri-Partners and TWDB datasets are the two sides of the comparison, not independent confirmations. Q7 no: no requirement stated for the effect; the peanut exception (surface kept moist in pegging, not captured by Kco) is an exception rather than a stated condition. Q9 no: 14-21% is a scenario sensitivity range, no dispersion or propagated uncertainty reported.

notes: Study is a hybrid of historical review (TWDB survey data, cited literature) and own analysis (FIR computation from Agri-Partners and TWDB data, scenario modelling of regional demand). Text appears complete.
